1.who: Hamdan Taha (حمدان طه) — “Archaeology in Palestine: The Palestinian Department of Antiquities and Cultural Heritage” · “The Current State of Archaeology in Palestine”
1.line: The founder of the Palestinian antiquities service explains what the national archaeological record holds, who keeps it, and what was lost.

1.who: Elihu Grant — “Ramallah: Signs of the Early Occupation of This and Other Sites”
1.line: The only archaeological article on Ramallah in the PEF series, gathering surface finds, tombs and the signs of the town’s earliest occupation.

1.who: Salah al-Houdalieh & Shadi Ghadban — “Agricultural Watchtowers in Al-Tireh Quarter and ʿAin Qinia Village”
1.line: A survey of the stone watchtowers in the terraced hills west of Ramallah, and the best way into that long-lived farming landscape.

1.who: مصطفى مراد الدباغ / Muṣṭafá Murād al-Dabbāgh — بلادنا فلسطين، الجزء الثامن، القسم الثاني: في ديار بيت المقدس
1.line: The standard Palestinian encyclopaedia, village by village, and the source for reading Rām as a shared Semitic root meaning height.

1.who: Marc Haber et al. — Levantine population genetics
1.line: Two free studies of continuity and mixture among Levantine peoples, read with care: nothing yet tests Palestinian Christian families directly.

2.who: Joseph A. Callaway & Robert E. Cooley — “A Salvage Excavation at Raddana, in Bireh”
2.line: An Iron Age village of pillared houses, silos, cisterns and terraces inside modern al-Bīra, with one of the highlands’ earliest alphabetic inscriptions.

2.who: Awni Shawamra (MOTA-Palestine) & Federico Cappella — “An Iron Age II Tomb with Phoenician Items at Khirbet Bir el-Kharayib”
2.line: A Palestinian Ministry salvage dig of an Iron Age tomb with Phoenician wares on the Nablus–Ramallah boundary, fully published and free.

2.who: Salah H. al-Houdalieh — the Ramallah province heritage-destruction corpus
2.line: Palestinian fieldwork on what building and looting have done to the district’s ancient sites, which doubles as a gazetteer of them.

2.who: Robert G. Hoyland — Arabia and the Arabs: From the Bronze Age to the Coming of Islam
2.line: The standard one-volume history of ancient Arabia, from Sabaʾ and Maʾrib to the caravan kingdoms, for weighing the migration story.

2.who: DASI — Digital Archive for the Study of pre-Islamic Arabian Inscriptions
2.pub: Università di Pisa / CNR · online, free
2.line: The Sabaic inscriptions, free to read, where the dam legend meets dated stone: the dam was real, and it broke more than once.

2.who: الهمداني / al-Hamdānī — صفة جزيرة العرب (ed. Muḥammad al-Akwaʿ)
2.line: A Yemeni geographer who walked the land describes Maʾrib and its country and the tribal map of the south the story starts from.

3.who: Vincent Michel — “El-Khadr, un complexe ecclésiastique byzantin et médiéval à Taybeh-Éphraïm (Cisjordanie)”
3.line: The definitive publication of the al-Khaḍr church complex at al-Ṭayyiba, the town the Gospel calls Ephraim, from a decade of French fieldwork.

3.who: Edward Robinson & Eli Smith — Biblical Researches in Palestine, vols. II and III
3.line: The 1838 travels from which the identification of the Gospel’s Ephraim with eṭ-Ṭaybeh became standard, with bearings across the neighbouring villages.

3.who: Salah al-Houdalieh — “Vandalised and Looted Rock-Cut Tombs of the Roman and Byzantine Periods: Saffa Village, Ramallah Province”
3.line: A Palestinian archaeologist records the rock-cut tombs of Roman and Byzantine Ṣaffā, west of Ramallah, and what looting has taken from them.

4.who: Irfan Shahîd — Byzantium and the Arabs, 7 volumes
4.pub: Dumbarton Oaks, Washington DC, 1984–2010 · free online
4.line: The standard, most far-reaching account of Ghassān as a Christian kingdom guarding Byzantium’s frontier, drawn from Greek, Syriac and Arabic sources.

4.who: Greg Fisher — Between Empires: Arabs, Romans, and Sasanians in Late Antiquity · Arabs and Empires before Islam (ed.)
4.line: The main counterweight to Shahîd, reading the Jafnids as a Roman-backed ruling family, with the original evidence set out and explained.

4.who: Norbert Nebes — “A New ʾAbraha Inscription from the Great Dam of Mārib”
4.pub: Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 34 (2004): 221–230
4.line: The inscription that dates Abraha’s repair of the Maʾrib dam to AD 548, and lays out when the dam actually broke.

4.who: ابن حزم / Ibn Ḥazm — جمهرة أنساب العرب · ابن الكلبي / Ibn al-Kalbī — جمهرة النسب
4.pub: d. 456/1064 and 204/819 · the two great compendia
4.line: The two founding books of Arab genealogy, which disagree with each other about where Ghassān begins, and show it plainly.

4.who: المسعودي / al-Masʿūdī — مروج الذهب ومعادن الجوهر
4.line: The classical telling of the dam’s bursting, the Azd dispersal and Ghassān’s road north to Syria, with its own list of kings.

4.who: Yasmine Zahran (ياسمين زهران, b. 1933 in Ramallah) — Ghassan Resurrected
4.line: A short, readable history of Ghassān by a Palestinian archaeologist born in Ramallah, best read beside Shahîd and Fisher.

4.who: Salah H. al-Houdalieh — “The Byzantine Eastern Church of Khirbet et-Tireh”
4.line: A Byzantine church inside Ramallah itself, with atrium, hall and over 400 square metres of mosaic, excavated by al-Quds University.

5.who: Hamdan Taha — “A Salvage Excavation at the ʿAbūdiyah Church in ʿAbūd, Samaria”
5.line: The district’s key dig: St Mary’s at ʿAbūd, with building phases from the fifth century on and an inscription recording a rebuilding in 1058.

5.who: إبراهيم خليل نيروز / Ibrāhīm Khalīl Nayrūz — كشف المفقود من كنائس عابود
5.line: A Ramallah historian recovers the churches and monasteries of ʿAbūd, one of the oldest Christian villages in the district.

5.who: Robert Schick — The Christian Communities of Palestine from Byzantine to Islamic Rule
5.line: Church by church, what happened to Palestine’s Christian buildings after 630: the core reference for whether the communities carried on.

5.who: The earlier geographers — al-Yaʿqūbī · Ibn Khurradādhbih · Ibn al-Faqīh · al-Iṣṭakhrī · Ibn Ḥawqal
5.line: The ninth- and tenth-century geographers give the frame for these hills: the districts of Filasṭīn, the post road, and farms watered only by rain.

5.who: المقدسي / al-Muqaddasī — أحسن التقاسيم في معرفة الأقاليم
5.pub: c. 985 · BGA III, ed. de Goeje, Leiden
5.line: A Jerusalemite describes his own hinterland: hills planted with trees and plains sown with grain, without irrigation and without rivers.

5.who: يحيى بن سعيد الأنطاكي / Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṭākī — the continuation of Eutychius
5.line: An Arabic chronicle of al-Ḥākim’s church destructions of 1009, counting them in thousands across the empire but naming almost none.

6.who: Denys Pringle — “Magna Mahumeria (al-Bira): The Archaeology of a Frankish New Town in Palestine”
6.line: The foundational study of Frankish al-Bīra: its street of vaulted houses, its church and its pools. Everything later builds on it.

6.who: عوني محمد محسن محليس / ʿAwnī Maḥlīs — البيرة في الفترة الصليبية: دراسة أثرية معمارية · سعيد البيشاوي / Saʿīd al-Bīshāwī on Crusader Beitunia
6.pub: MA thesis, Al-Quds University, 2000 · al-Quds University, 2023
6.line: The Palestinian scholarship on Crusader al-Bīra and Beitunia, the only substantial Arabic study of the site and rarely cited in English.

6.who: Saʿīd Aljoumani, Zahir Bhalloo & Konrad Hirschler — The Ḥaram al-Sharīf Documents: A New Corpus
6.line: Newly catalogued Jerusalem documents, among them a debt of 1374 owed by a Christian of Jifnā, the earliest named Christian of this district.

6.who: ياقوت الحموي / Yāqūt al-Ḥamawī — معجم البلدان (Muʿjam al-buldān)
6.line: An eyewitness geographer on al-Bīra after Saladin and on ʿAyn Yabrūd’s waqf, vines and olives: the richest text for these hills.

6.who: ابن فضل الله العمري / Ibn Faḍl Allāh al-ʿUmarī — مسالك الأبصار في ممالك الأمصار
6.line: The earliest substantial statement on the people of this country: settled Arab clans in Wādī Banī Zayd, and endowments in the district.

6.who: مجير الدين العليمي / Mujīr al-Dīn al-ʿUlaymī — الأنس الجليل بتاريخ القدس والخليل
6.line: The Jerusalem historian who draws the district’s Mamluk border, showing why Ramallah’s site sat on a seam the record passes over.

6.who: يوسف غوانمة / Yūsuf Ghawānma — the Mamluk and Ayyubid history of southern Transjordan
6.pub: Arabic studies of Ayyubid and Mamluk Karak and Jerusalem
6.line: A Jordanian historian on Karak’s Christians and their crossings to Jerusalem, and on the villages of the Mamluk Jerusalem governorate.

7.who: Azeez Shaheen — Ramallah: Its History and Its Genealogies (كشف النقاب عن الجدود والأنساب في مدينة رام الله)
7.line: The foundation of the family tree, built on 1970s fieldwork, printing the family accounts of 1953 and 1954 of the coming from Karak.

7.who: Sameeh Hammoudeh — “New Light on Ramallah’s Origins in the Ottoman Period”
7.line: Start here: Ottoman registers and court records retell the founding, with the Christian families of Bayt Jālā counted at Ramallah by 1562.

7.who: محمد عدنان البخيت ونوفان رجا السوارية — دفتر مفصل لواء القدس الشريف
7.line: The Jerusalem tax registers in Arabic with commentary, including the register of 1562 against which the founding story can be tested.

7.who: Naseeb Shaheen — A Pictorial History of Ramallah
7.line: The great illustrated history of the town by a Ramallah-born scholar, which prints the family accounts of Rāshid’s road from Karak.

7.who: يوسف جرجس قدورة / Yūsuf Jurjis Qadūrah — تاريخ مدينة رام الله (Tārīkh madīnat Rām Allāh)
7.line: The first full Arabic history of the town, written in the American diaspora; every later author argues with its account of the founding.

7.who: يحيى عيسى الفرحان / Yaḥyá ʻĪsá al-Farḥān — قصة مدينة رام الله والبيرة (Qiṣṣat madīnat Rām Allāh wa-al-Bīrah)
7.line: The most widely read short Arabic history of the twin towns, written in exile for everyone, and free to download.

7.who: Munther J. Haddadin (منذر حدادين) — دولة الغساسنة: أصيلها ورحيلها (The Ghassanid State: Its Origin and Its Departure)
7.line: A Jordanian Ḥaddādīn author traces the Azd north from Maʾrib to the Ghassānid founding, and holds his own clan to descend from them.

8.who: Azeez Shaheen — Ramallah: Its History and Its Genealogies (كشف النقاب عن الجدود والأنساب في مدينة رام الله)
8.line: Every clan and line from the founders, the newcomers and their arrival dates, and the town’s feuds, gathered from the families themselves.

8.who: سميح حمودة / Samīḥ Ḥammūdah — رام الله العثمانية: دراسات في تاريخها الاجتماعي، ١٥١٧–١٩١٨ (Rām Allāh al-ʻUthmānīyah)
8.line: The scholarly benchmark: court records, tax registers and church archives rebuild Ottoman Ramallah’s land, clans and Christian–Muslim life.

8.who: Sameeh Hammoudeh — “New Light on Ramallah’s Origins in the Ottoman Period”
8.line: Names the Muslim households already at Ramallah before the Christians came, and shows exactly which registers to read.
Patriarchate documents of 1706 and 1709 paying a priest at Ramallah to teach the children and listing the Orthodox parishes.

8.who: سلسلة سجلات المحاكم الشرعية — سجلات محكمة القدس, ed. إبراهيم ربايعة / Ibrāhīm Rabāyiʿah
8.line: Case-by-case summaries of the Jerusalem court registers, including a 1565 boundary dispute over Ramallah settled by a waqf deed of 1279.

8.who: Felicita Tramontana — Passages of Faith: Conversion in Palestinian Villages (17th Century)
8.line: The missing seventeenth century: village by village, how Christians of Ramallah, Jifnā, al-Ṭayyiba and their neighbours held their faith or changed it.

8.who: سعاد العامري / Suad Amiry — عمارة قرى الكراسي: من تاريخ الإقطاع في ريف فلسطين في القرنين الثامن عشر والتاسع عشر (Throne Village Architecture)
8.line: The throne villages of the Banī Zayd hills and the palaces of their shaykhly families, the world around Ramallah before the municipality.

9.who: Azeez Shaheen — Ramallah: Its History and Its Genealogies (كشف النقاب عن الجدود والأنساب في مدينة رام الله)
9.line: The town’s own record of its churches, schools, first doctors, guest houses, weddings and feasts, set down by a son of Ramallah.

9.who: Edward Robinson & Eli Smith — Biblical Researches in Palestine, vols. II and III
9.line: Robinson’s 1838 visit is the earliest close description of Ram-Allah and its Greek-rite Christians, thirty years before the Quaker mission.

9.who: Beshara Doumani — Rediscovering Palestine: Merchants and Peasants in Jabal Nablus, 1700–1900
9.line: The model study of Ottoman Palestinian rural society, merchants, peasants and notable houses, reaching into the Banī Zayd hills around Ramallah.

9.who: سميح حمودة / Samīḥ Ḥammūdah — رام الله العثمانية: دراسات في تاريخها الاجتماعي، ١٥١٧–١٩١٨ (Rām Allāh al-ʻUthmānīyah)
9.line: Ottoman Ramallah’s social history to 1918, from court records and church archives, reaching into the century of the new churches and schools.

9.who: نظمي الجعبة وخلدون بشارة / Nazmi al-Jubeh & Khaldun Bshara — رام الله: عمارة وتاريخ (Ramallah: Architecture and History)
9.line: The definitive study of the old town’s buildings, house by house, with archival photographs, measured plans and an urban history.

9.who: Riwaq Registry of Historic Buildings in Palestine — Ramallah & al-Bireh district
9.line: A searchable record of the old town’s courtyard houses, churches and Ottoman core, with a report for each building.

9.who: Lisa Taraki — “Ordinary Lives: A Small-town Middle Class at the Turn of the Twentieth Century”
9.line: How mission schooling, the pilgrim trade and emigration made a small-town middle class, built from family histories, diaries and photographs.

10.who: Azeez Shaheen — Ramallah: Its History and Its Genealogies (كشف النقاب عن الجدود والأنساب في مدينة رام الله)
10.line: The first sailings to America, the new municipality, the last big fight, the war years and the town’s societies, as Ramallah remembers them.

10.who: Khalil Totah, ed. Thomas M. Ricks — Turbulent Times in Palestine: The Diaries of Khalil Totah, 1886–1955
10.line: The diaries of the Ramallah-born head of the Friends Boys School, the most important record of the town’s schools under the Mandate.

10.who: Elihu Grant — The Peasantry of Palestine: The Life, Manners and Customs of the Village
10.line: A Friends School principal’s portrait of village life around 1901–04, with observations, photographs and proverbs drawn mostly from Ramallah.

10.who: J. B. Barron (ed.) — Palestine: Report and General Abstracts of the Census of 1922
10.line: The first modern count of the town and every village of its sub-district, by religion and sex, free to read.

10.who: Saleh Abdel Jawad — “Landed Property, Palestinian Migration to America and the Emergence of a New Local Leadership: al-Bireh 1919–1947”
10.line: How money sent home from America reshaped land and leadership in al-Bīra, with Ramallah alongside, from the first emigration waves.

10.who: Nadim Bawalsa — Transnational Palestine: Migration and the Right of Return before 1948
10.line: The central study of Palestinian emigrants in the Americas, many from Ramallah, and of how the Mandate shut them out of citizenship.

10.pub: Founded by Boulos Shehadeh · Internet Archive, searchable
10.line: A Ramallah man’s newspaper, full of municipal news, schools, churches and emigration: the richest Arabic source for the Mandate town.

11.who: Azeez Shaheen — Ramallah: Its History and Its Genealogies (كشف النقاب عن الجدود والأنساب في مدينة رام الله)
11.line: The great influx of 1948, the hard years after, and the diaspora societies that built a hospital, told from inside the town.

11.who: Joseph Jiryes Cadora (Yūsuf Jurjis Qadūrah), trans. Samira Meghdessian — Remembering Ramallah: A Preservation of History
11.line: The first English translation of the town’s first full history, written in 1954 and now the easiest diaspora classic to read.

11.who: Lisa Taraki — “Enclave Micropolis: The Paradoxical Case of Ramallah/al-Bireh”
11.line: The standard account of Ramallah and al-Bīra as a small twin town pushed into a capital’s role, drawing on the town’s own emigration figures.

11.who: سميح حمودة / Sameeh Hammoudeh — اللاجئون الفلسطينيون لمخيم قدورة في رام الله خلال الحقبة الأردنية (١٩٤٨–١٩٦٧)
11.line: A social history of Qaddura camp under Jordan: how it formed, how it was run, and how refugees and the town lived together.

11.who: عادل ح. يحيى / Adel H. Yahya — قصة مخيم الجلزون: تاريخ شفوي
11.line: The refugees of Jalazone tell their own story: the villages they left in 1948, the making of the camp and life afterwards.

11.who: Adel H. Yahya — The Palestinian Refugees 1948–1998: An Oral History
11.line: Refugees settled in the Ramallah and al-Bīra camps, al-Amʿari, Qaddura and Jalazone, remember fifty years in their own words.

11.who: Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question (palquest)
11.pub: Institute for Palestine Studies & The Palestinian Museum · online
11.line: Carefully sourced Palestinian entries on places and events, including the camps, for checking our story against the scholarly consensus.

12.who: Azeez Shaheen — Ramallah: Its History and Its Genealogies (كشف النقاب عن الجدود والأنساب في مدينة رام الله)
12.line: The record closes here: emigration counted decade by decade and the town under occupation, set down by a man born in 1894.

12.who: PCBS — Census 2017: Final Results Summary, Ramallah and al-Bireh Governorate
12.line: The governorate counted in 1997, 2007 and 2017 on the same terms: the place to start for any number about today’s city.

12.who: Lisa Taraki — “Enclave Micropolis: The Paradoxical Case of Ramallah/al-Bireh”
12.line: The piece everything since argues with, on how an enclosed twin town became the de facto capital after Oslo.

12.who: حسين الريماوي / Ḥusayn al-Rīmāwī — التطور التاريخي وتحليل التركيب الداخلي لمدينتي رام الله والبيرة: دراسة في جغرافية المدن
12.pub: Journal of the Social Sciences (Kuwait) 35:4 (2007) · free
12.line: The most important Arabic article on the twin cities: how they grew, phase by phase, and how they are laid out today.

12.who: Yaser Mohammed Sarhan Kassab — “Internal Immigration to Ramallah and al-Bireh Cities” / الهجرة الداخلية إلى مدينتي رام الله والبيرة
12.line: The movement from village to city that built modern Ramallah and al-Bīra, with full demographic tables for the twentieth century.

12.who: Mourid Barghouti, trans. Ahdaf Soueif, foreword Edward W. Said — I Saw Ramallah
12.line: A poet’s return to Ramallah and Deir Ghassāna after thirty years of exile, the canonical literary account of the district.

12.who: Lisa Taraki (ed.) — Living Palestine: Family Survival, Resistance, and Mobility under Occupation
12.line: Birzeit scholars on how Ramallah and al-Bīra families got by, resisted and moved under occupation, from local surveys and fieldwork.
